quarterly_data.signal: THE HBF CONSORTIUM NOW HAS TWO MANUFACTURERS AND TWO USERS (CFO): 'The first thing we needed to do was build a consortium. When we announced that we are working on HBF, we saw a few companies raise their hand, particularly, SK hynix called us, and they said they were interested in partnering with us in developing the standard. We are not developing products together, we are just developing standards.' Then: 'Since then, Google and Meta joined the consortium, right? You have two manufacturers, and you have two potential or two users of this technology.' Next milestone is silicon at customers: 'The next step is to get products in our customers' hands. What we will do in 2027, and then we'll see from there.' Function: HBF 'has the ability to get much closer to the CPU, GPU' to hold the inference memory (KV cache) - 'You solve a problem without any bandwidth trade-offs, and you get a lot more density into it.'
quarterly_data.figure: products in customers' hands in 2027; two manufacturers and two users in the consortium

quarterly_data.signal: HBF IS FUNDED ONLY AT THE OPEX LINE AND IS NOT IN THE LONG-TERM MODEL (CFO): 'we cover the OpEx for HBF. We don't have the revenue, the gross margin, the gross profit, and the CapEx. We need to figure that out... we need just a little bit more time to understand the customer's acceptance, their needs, how fast they're willing to go.' The manufacturing base is already in place, which caps the incremental capital: 'the foundation is BiCS technology. This is BiCS8. It's not that we need to invent a new node... It can be produced in existing tools.' R&D is funded across the jointly agreed BiCS program with Kioxia, the product organisation for enterprise SSDs and client, and 'two big bets. One is HBF and the other one is this new memory technology that was briefly discussed by Alper in the Analyst Day.'

WHO THE NBM CUSTOMERS ARE, AND WHAT AN NBM REQUIRES (CFO): the signed book is concentrated in hyperscalers - 'three U.S. hyperscalers' - plus, as disclosed at the Analyst Day, 'at least one customer in the edge, right? We did not say who it was but we are very excited about that.' The first NBM was signed 'I think was in January' and was deliberately short and with a strategic customer while Sandisk was 'taking small steps and really warming up and learning on how to do this.' Two contracts have since been amended: 'One of them extended the duration, and the other one just added a ton of volume to the NBM that we had initially signed... The only things that changed in the new contract were quantities, and we did adjust price to the prices that we thought were attractive for them and attractive for us.' Any new NBM, including edge customers asking for long-term agreements, must carry all four elements: 'There has to be a time commitment, there has to be a volume commitment, there has to be price, and there has to be a financial guarantee.'
quarterly_data.figure: three U.S. hyperscalers plus at least one edge customer; first NBM signed in January; two contracts changed

quarterly_data.signal: SUPPLY GROWTH COMES ENTIRELY FROM NODE TRANSITIONS - NO NEW WAFERS (CFO): asked how much of mid-to-high-teens bit growth is mix versus wafers, the CFO said 'I would say it is 100% driven by node transition... going forward, we do not expect that we will need any wafer additions to supply the market. All of this is driven by more efficient, more productive wafers where you can fit in more bits.' Sandisk has been producing fewer wafers over the years, underutilised its fabs about 18 months ago and has since ramped back up. CBA/direct bonding is framed as an R&D-productivity tool (innovate on the array or the CMOS independently), 'but that is not how we drive productivity on the wafer. It is the array itself.' Capacity spending follows the same mid-to-high-teens target: 'The dollar amount will increase... but still within the percentages that we talked about, percentage of revenue', because the cheapest transitions (into tools freed up by the earlier underutilisation) were done first.
quarterly_data.figure: 100% driven by node transition; no wafer additions needed to supply the market

quarterly_data.signal: EDGE UNITS TURN POSITIVE IN 2027 AFTER THE LOW-END MODELS ARE CULLED (CFO): 'the edge customers are adjusting to the fact that memory was subsidized, and now it's no longer being subsidized... the low-end models, right, they are just not viable anymore. And they are really shifting towards a higher performing, medium to higher performing models.' The forward call: 'once you eliminate the lower-end models, we believe that next year we should expect to see low single-digit unit growth and maybe a little bit more on content growth. Just particularly focused on the models that will remain, which are the medium and the higher end.' AI at the edge is not yet a content driver - 'AI could be a driver of replacement of old PCs, for example, but not a major factor so far. I would see it more on the data center.'
quarterly_data.figure: low single-digit unit growth next year and maybe a little bit more on content growth

quarterly_data.signal: MIX TO DATA CENTER RAISES UNIT COST EVEN AS MARGINS RISE - NON-MEMORY COST IS CLIMBING (CFO): 'as you move more of your business to data center, those products are more costly per unit. But the gross margins are still very interesting and attractive, but the unit cost could be higher because there is more components, more DRAM, more components in general. So there will be a mixed element of that, and DRAM and just as a few other components have increased in cost. So what we call non-memory cost keeps on going up.' Offsetting that, the CFO named capital efficiency per incremental bit as the single most important cost advantage: 'over time, we've been consistently spending less CapEx per additional bit, which makes us very competitive, because then that flows through obviously lower depreciation, lower unit cost.'

contracts.signal: The CFO described how the HBF partnership started and where it now stands: 'SK hynix called us, and they said they were interested in partnering with us in developing the standard. We are not developing products together, we are just developing standards. SK hynix obviously knows a few things about HBM, being one of the largest producers of HBM... Having two strong players partnered together made a ton of sense.' The consortium has since widened - 'Since then, Google and Meta joined the consortium' - giving it two manufacturers and two prospective users, with product going into customers' hands in 2027.
